title: Could You Survive a Year as a Medieval Peasant? (1348)
idea: What if you had to survive one year as a medieval English peasant in 1348
question: Would you have survived 1348? What's the first modern thing you'd miss?

scenes.narration: It's the morning of March twenty-fifth, 1348, and you just woke up on a pile of straw.

claims.text: Stan waking up in 1348 is a dramatization
claims.source: Narrative device

scenes.narration: Congratulations. You are a medieval peasant, and your mission is simple: survive one year.
Oh, and happy New Year! In medieval England, the year officially started on March twenty-fifth.

overlays.text: From the 1100s until 1752, England's legal year began on 25 March (Lady Day).
overlays.source: Royal Museums Greenwich, 'When did New Year's Day change to 1 January?'

claims.text: England's civil/legal year began on 25 March until 1752
claims.source: Royal Museums Greenwich, 'When did New Year's Day change to 1 January?'

scenes.narration: Now, I'm going to be honest with you. Of all the years you could have picked…
Here's how this works: every chapter, Stan's survival odds go up or down, depending on what life throws at him.
this is the worst one. By the end of it, a huge part of England will be dead.

claims.text: The Black Death reached England in 1348
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: So let's see what it takes to make it through 1348, one season at a time. Ready? Let's go.
Let's start with your house. It's one room, built from a wooden frame packed with mud and straw.

claims.text: Peasant houses were timber-framed with wattle-and-daub walls and thatched roofs
claims.source: English Heritage, 'Medieval peasant houses'

scenes.narration: There's no chimney. The fire burns in the middle of the floor, and the smoke just… finds its way out.

claims.text: Most peasant houses had an open central hearth and no chimney
claims.source: English Heritage, 'Medieval peasant houses'

scenes.narration: The floor is packed earth covered in straw, which is cozy, right up until you meet the rats.
And you're not alone. Meet your wife, Maud, and your son, Wat.

claims.text: Stan's family is fictional
claims.source: Narrative device

scenes.narration: Also living with you: a pig, a few chickens, and, if you're lucky, a cow.
In many longhouses, the animals lived at one end of the building. Their body heat kept everyone warm.

overlays.text: Longhouses sheltered people and livestock under one roof, often with a cross-passage between them.
overlays.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

claims.text: In some regions peasants lived in longhouses shared with livestock
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: The smell? Let's just say you stop noticing it after a week.
Here's the first bad news. You don't really own anything. Not the land, not the house…
and in a way, not even yourself. Because this guy does.

claims.text: Sir Hugh is a fictional lord
claims.source: Narrative device

scenes.narration: You're a villein, an unfree peasant. You're bound to Sir Hugh's manor, and you can't just leave.

say.text: Where do you think you're going?

claims.text: Villeins were unfree tenants legally bound to their lord's manor
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: In exchange for your strips of land, you owe him work. Often two or three days a week, every week.

claims.text: Villeins typically owed 'week-work' on the lord's demesne, often 2-3 days per week
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937); Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: That's free labor on his fields, called the demesne, while your own crops wait.

claims.text: The lord's demesne was farmed using villeins' labor services
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: Making sure you actually show up is the reeve, a fellow peasant with a clipboard energy.

claims.text: The reeve was a villager chosen to oversee work on the manor
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: And the fees. Oh, the fees. Want your daughter to marry? Pay the lord a fine, called merchet.

claims.text: Merchet was a fine paid to the lord when an unfree woman married
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: When you die, he takes your best animal. That one is called heriot.

claims.text: Heriot: on a tenant's death the lord took the best beast
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: Need flour? You must grind your grain at his mill, and he keeps a cut of it.

claims.text: Tenants were often obliged to use the lord's mill and pay a toll (multure) in grain
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: And then there's the Church, which takes a tithe: one tenth of everything you produce.

claims.text: A tithe of one tenth of produce was owed to the Church
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Break the rules, and you'll end up in the manor court, where your own neighbors help decide your fine.

claims.text: Manor courts, with juries of tenants, fined villagers for breaches of custom
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: Typical crimes? Letting your pig wander into the lord's crops, or brewing ale that's too weak.

claims.text: Common manor-court offences included straying animals and breaches of the assize of ale
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: And if someone shouts that a crime has happened, everyone must drop what they're doing and chase the culprit.

claims.text: The 'hue and cry' obliged villagers to pursue suspected criminals
claims.source: Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)

scenes.narration: Add it all up, and a big share of your work never feeds your own family.

overlays.title: Where your year's effort goes (rough idea)

claims.text: Labor services, rents, fines and tithe took a large share of a villein's output; exact shares varied by manor
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Some of your rent isn't even paid in money. It's paid in hens at Christmas and eggs at Easter.

claims.text: Rents in kind such as 'Christmas hens' and Easter eggs were common manorial dues
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: Your one legal escape? Run to a chartered town and live there for a year and a day without being caught. Then you're free.

overlays.text: A villein who lived unclaimed in a privileged town for a year and a day could gain his freedom.
overlays.source: Glanvill, Treatise on the Laws of England (c. 1188)

claims.text: A villein residing unclaimed for a year and a day in a privileged town could become free
claims.source: Glanvill, Treatise on the Laws of England (c. 1188)

scenes.narration: Still, it's not all misery. Sundays and dozens of holy days are days off from field work.

overlays.text: Sundays plus dozens of church feast days were holidays.
overlays.source: Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)

claims.text: Sundays and many holy days (feast days) were rest days
claims.source: Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)

scenes.narration: It's spring, so it's time to plough. Your village farms huge open fields divided into long strips.

claims.text: Many English villages farmed open fields divided into strips
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Your strips are scattered all over, so the good soil and the bad soil get shared around.

claims.text: A peasant's holding was scattered in strips across the fields
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: A typical villein family might hold around thirty acres, but plenty of families had much less.

claims.text: A standard villein holding (virgate/yardland) was often around 30 acres, varying by region; many held half that or less
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002); H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: Nobody owns enough oxen to pull a heavy plough alone, so neighbors share their animals.

claims.text: Plough teams were often assembled by several tenants pooling their oxen
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Each year, one big field rests, called fallow, so the soil can recover.

claims.text: Crop rotation with a fallow field (two- and three-field systems) was common
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: You work from sunrise until the light is gone. So, what's for lunch?
Pottage. A thick stew of grains, peas, beans and whatever vegetables are growing.

claims.text: Pottage of grains and pulses was a staple of the peasant diet
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Tomorrow? Pottage. The day after? You guessed it.
Add dark bread made from rye or barley, and a little cheese, eggs, or bacon when you can get them.

claims.text: Bread from rye, barley or mixed grains, with some dairy, eggs and occasional bacon
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: And to drink? Ale. Lots of it. Weak, cloudy ale was a daily food, not a party drink.

overlays.text: Ale was a staple: brewed mostly by women ('alewives') and regulated by the Assize of Bread and Ale.
overlays.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

claims.text: Ale was a dietary staple, commonly brewed by women
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

claims.text: The Assize of Bread and Ale regulated prices and quality
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: People did drink water too. But ale was safer, tastier, and it filled you up.

overlays.text: Myth: "medieval people never drank water" — they did.

claims.text: Medieval people did drink water; ale was nonetheless a staple calorie source
claims.source: Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)

scenes.narration: Maud works just as hard as you. She brews, spins wool, makes cheese, keeps the animals, and helps in the fields.

claims.text: Peasant women brewed, spun, made dairy produce, tended livestock and worked in the fields
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937); Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: And Wat? At seven, he's already working: collecting firewood, minding geese, and scaring birds off the seeds.

claims.text: Children did tasks such as gathering fuel, tending animals and bird-scaring
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Your clothes are simple: a wool tunic, linen underneath, and a hood. You own maybe two outfits.

claims.text: Peasants wore woollen outer garments over linen undergarments
claims.source: Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)

scenes.narration: And then there's the hungry gap: late spring, when last year's food is running out, and the new crops aren't ready yet.

claims.text: Late spring/early summer was the leanest time before the new harvest
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Your parents remember the Great Famine of 1315 to 1317. Years of rain, rotting crops, and hunger.

claims.text: The Great Famine of 1315-1317 followed years of torrential rain and failed harvests
claims.source: William Chester Jordan, The Great Famine (Princeton, 1996)

scenes.narration: So every spring, you plant, you pray, and you hope the weather behaves.
Quick myth check. You've probably heard that medieval people never washed. Not true.
scenes.chapter: Wait… Were They Really That Dirty?

scenes.narration: Washing your hands and face every morning was normal, and towns had public bathhouses, called stews.

claims.text: Daily washing of hands and face was customary; towns had public bathhouses ('stews')
claims.source: Katherine Harvey, The Fires of Lust / Smithsonian, 'Medieval people did bathe'; Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)

scenes.narration: And the idea that everyone died at thirty? That average is dragged down by children.

claims.text: Low average life expectancy at birth was driven by high infant and child mortality
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Sadly, around one in three children didn't reach adulthood. But if you did, reaching your fifties or sixties was normal.

overlays.caption: ≈ 1 in 3 children didn't make it to adulthood

claims.text: Roughly a third of children may have died before adulthood; adults commonly lived into their 50s-60s
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002); Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)

scenes.narration: So, rule one of surviving 1348: get past childhood. Good news: you already did.
Summer. The crops are growing, the hay needs cutting, and the village is busy.
But around the end of June, a ship docks at Melcombe, a port in Dorset.

claims.text: The Black Death arrived in England at Melcombe (Weymouth), Dorset, in June 1348
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: On board is something nobody can see: plague. The Black Death has reached England.

claims.text: Plague (the Black Death) spread through England from summer 1348
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: It's caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas that live on rats, and on people.

claims.text: Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, transmitted by fleas from rats; human-to-human spread (including via human fleas/lice and pneumonic form) is also discussed by historians
claims.source: CDC, 'Plague: symptoms and transmission'; Ole J. Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353 (Boydell, 2004)

scenes.narration: Of course, nobody in 1348 knows that. Doctors blame bad air, the stars, or God's anger.

claims.text: Contemporaries blamed corrupted air (miasma), planetary conjunctions and divine punishment
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: And no, the famous beaked plague doctor mask wasn't around yet. That shows up in the sixteen hundreds.

overlays.text: The beaked costume is described in the 1600s, not 1348.
overlays.source: British Library, 'Medieval medicine and the plague doctor'

claims.text: The beaked plague-doctor costume dates from the 17th century
claims.source: British Library, 'Medieval medicine and the plague doctor'

scenes.narration: By July the plague is spreading inland. Village by village, the news arrives before the disease does.

claims.text: Plague spread from Dorset across southern England through summer and autumn 1348
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: It reaches Bristol in August, and London by the autumn. Wherever people travel, it travels too.

claims.text: Plague reached Bristol by August 1348 and London by autumn 1348
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994); Ole J. Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353 (Boydell, 2004)

scenes.narration: The symptoms are terrifying: fever, and painful swellings called buboes in the armpits or groin.

claims.text: Bubonic plague causes fever and swollen lymph nodes (buboes) in groin, armpit or neck
claims.source: CDC, 'Plague: symptoms and transmission'

scenes.narration: Many of the sick die within a week. Some recover. Nobody knows why.

claims.text: Many bubonic plague victims died within about a week; some survived
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: Stan's family stays home, prays, and waits. Every cough in the night sounds like a death sentence.
By autumn, the plague is in your village. Your neighbor goes first. Then the priest.

claims.text: Parish clergy, who visited the dying, suffered very high death rates
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: People try everything. Processions, prayers, bonfires, fleeing to the countryside. Nothing seems to work.

claims.text: Responses included religious processions, prayer and flight
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: Graveyards fill up so fast that new burial grounds are opened, like the one at East Smithfield in London.

overlays.text: East Smithfield, London: an emergency cemetery opened for plague victims in 1348-49.

claims.text: East Smithfield was an emergency Black Death cemetery in London (1348-49)
claims.source: Museum of London Archaeology

scenes.narration: Across England, somewhere between a third and a half of the population dies. Possibly more.

overlays.caption: Out of every 10 people, 3 to 5 died

claims.text: Estimates of Black Death mortality in England range from about a third to a half or more; Benedictow argues for ~60%
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994); Ole J. Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353 (Boydell, 2004)

scenes.narration: Whole families vanish. Some villages are simply abandoned.

claims.text: Some settlements were deserted after the plague, though many 'lost villages' declined over a longer period
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: And Stan? Stan gets lucky. Maud and Wat too. Nobody really knows why some survived.

claims.text: Stan's family surviving is fictional
claims.source: Narrative device

scenes.narration: Now it's harvest time, the most important weeks of the year. But half the workers are gone.
scenes.chapter: Autumn: The Harvest Nobody Can Bring In

scenes.narration: Chroniclers describe crops rotting in the fields and animals wandering with nobody to look after them.

overlays.text: Sheep and cattle strayed through the fields and among the crops, and there was no one to drive them off.

claims.text: Henry Knighton described livestock wandering untended after the plague
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994)

scenes.narration: Which means, for the first time in your life, you have something the lord desperately needs.
Your labor. Workers are suddenly rare, so they start demanding higher wages.

say.text: Double pay. Or do it yourself.

claims.text: After the Black Death labor shortages pushed wages sharply upward
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: The government panics. In 1349, a new law tries to freeze wages at pre-plague levels.

overlays.text: The Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to cap wages.
overlays.source: Ordinance of Labourers (1349) & Statute of Labourers (1351), UK Parliament

claims.text: The Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and Statute of Labourers (1351) attempted to fix wages at pre-plague levels
claims.source: Ordinance of Labourers (1349) & Statute of Labourers (1351), UK Parliament

scenes.narration: On many manors, lords also start swapping your labor services for a simple money rent. Fewer days working his fields.

claims.text: After the Black Death labor services were increasingly commuted to money rents
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: It doesn't really work. Lords quietly break it themselves, because otherwise their crops rot.

claims.text: Wage laws were widely evaded as employers competed for scarce labor
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: There's also empty land now. Holdings whose families died are suddenly available, and some survivors grab them.

claims.text: Vacant holdings after the plague were taken up by survivors, often on better terms
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: It's a strange feeling. The worst year in memory is also the first time peasants hold some real power.
Before winter, you thresh the grain, store it, and pay your tithe. Again.
November is slaughter month. Animals you can't feed through winter are killed, and their meat is salted.

claims.text: Livestock were slaughtered in late autumn and the meat salted or smoked for winter
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: Winter is long, dark and cold. The whole family sleeps close together by the fire.
But then comes the best part of the year: Christmas. Twelve whole days of it.

claims.text: The twelve days of Christmas were a major holiday period
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: Work on the lord's land stops, and on many manors, the lord even provides a feast for his tenants.

claims.text: On many manors labor services were suspended at Christmas and lords provided a feast (sometimes the tenants contributed food)
claims.source: H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)

scenes.narration: For a few days, there's meat, ale, and music. And then, slowly, the light returns.
The rest of winter is quiet work indoors: mending tools, spinning, telling stories by the fire, and waiting for spring.

claims.text: Winter was used for indoor work such as repairs and spinning
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: March twenty-fourth, 1349. The last day of your year. Let's check the score.
You survived the work, the fees, the pottage, the winter, and the deadliest pandemic in European history.

claims.text: The Black Death is considered the deadliest pandemic in recorded European history
claims.source: Ole J. Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353 (Boydell, 2004)

scenes.narration: Final tally: a penny or two a day before the plague, and up to three pennies after. Around three hundred bowls of pottage. And one very lucky family.

claims.text: Unskilled daily wages of roughly 1-2d before 1348 rose substantially afterwards
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: And here's the twist. Your world is about to change. With so few workers left, peasants start to push back.

claims.text: Post-plague labor scarcity strengthened peasants' bargaining position
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: In 1381, they rise up in the Peasants' Revolt. Within a few generations, serfdom in England fades away.

claims.text: The Peasants' Revolt took place in 1381
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

claims.text: Villeinage largely disappeared in England by the 1500s
claims.source: Christopher Dyer, Making a Living in the Middle Ages (Yale, 2002)

scenes.narration: So, would you have survived 1348? And what's the first modern thing you'd miss?
Tell me in the comments. And if you enjoyed surviving with Stan, subscribe. Next time, we go somewhere even worse.

metadata.title: Could You Survive a Year as a Medieval Peasant? (1348)
metadata.description_intro:
You wake up on March 25th, 1348 — New Year's Day in medieval England — as Stan, an unfree peasant on a manor in Dorset. Your mission: survive one year. You'll deal with a lord who owns your labor, the tithe, endless pottage, the harvest… and the Black Death, which lands in England that very summer.

A stickman history story with real facts and sources.
metadata.pinned_comment: Would you have survived 1348? 🤔 And what's the first modern thing you'd miss? Mine is definitely not-pottage. 👇
